{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Ball-simplex matrix games: arbitrary randomized two-sided matrix-vector queries\par}\vspace{5pt}


\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{CV\_\allowbreak{}S\_\allowbreak{}MG\_\allowbreak{}RANDOM\_\allowbreak{}BALL}



Minimax optimization



Normalized ball-simplex matrix games with arbitrary randomized two-sided matvec queries. Exact zero and one-query endpoints are established by local proofs; the high-dimensional epsilon-dependent randomized lower remains excluded. A full-domain KOS v3 upper is combined with exact reconstruction under the randomized target quantity.



\textbf{Status.} Polynomial gap present



\textbf{TASK tags.} task family: Matrix computation; task family: Minimax



\textbf{MODEL tags.} geometry: Ball simplex; geometry: Compact geometry



\textbf{ORACLE tags.} feedback quality: Exact; interface family: Two sided real queries; operation: Two sided matvec; public information: Hidden objects explicitly declared; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared



\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: Explicitly no additional algorithm restrictions; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed; restriction: No additional zero-respecting restriction explicitly imposed



\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required; object: Point



\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: Saddle-point gap



\textbf{GUARANTEE tags.} aggregation: Per instance; confidence: Fixed numerical success / failure probability; mode: Probability; quantifier: Algorithm before instance; randomness: Algorithm private seed



\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} accounting: Joint coordinates retained; budget: Fixed worst-case budget; measure: N matvec pair; setup: Initialization included



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}



\AtlasMath{\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in\Delta_m}y^\top Ax,\quad A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.}




\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}


Assume \AtlasInlineMath{A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}, \AtlasInlineMath{B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}}, and \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta_m=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y_i\ge0,\ \mathbf1^\top y=1\}}. Also \AtlasInlineMath{X=B_2^n}, with each row satisfying \AtlasInlineMath{\|A_{i,:}\|_2\le1}.



The dimensions \AtlasInlineMath{m,n} are public and the matrix is hidden. Both strategy domains are compact and convex, ensuring a saddle point.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}


Public inputs include matrix dimensions \AtlasInlineMath{m,n} and tolerance \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}, together with the declared initial point and feasible-set information. The hidden function, operator, or matrix has no disclosed analytic representation.




\AtlasMath{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\longmapsto(Ax,A^\top y)}




A pair of left and right matrix products forms one bundled call. Responses are exact, and query vectors need not belong to the strategy domains.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}


Return \AtlasInlineMath{(\widehat{x},\widehat{y})\in X\times\Delta_m}.



The output may be any measurable postprocessing of the history, including an unqueried point, average, or convex combination. It must satisfy the stated domain and feasibility requirements; no additional function value or computable certificate is required.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}



\AtlasMath{\max_{v\in\Delta_m}v^\top A\widehat{x}-\min_{u\in X}\widehat{y}^\top Au}




The global gap is finite and nonnegative, and at most \AtlasInlineMath{2} on the normalized class.



The complete gap can be as large as 2 for an arbitrary pair, but the public choice \AtlasInlineMath{x=0} gives gap at most 1 for every matrix. The exact zero-query threshold for this randomized target is therefore \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon=1}.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}


A bundled two-sided call costs \AtlasInlineMath{N_{\rm matvec}}. A single right or transpose product can be simulated by setting the other input to zero.



Use a fixed worst-case budget: calls never exceed the prespecified \AtlasInlineMath{N} on any instance or random execution path. Earlier stopping within the budget is permitted.



Count all information calls for one instance and one requested accuracy, including initialization. Exact-real arithmetic, storage, and solving known models from public inputs and returned data are uncharged. This query-complexity quantity does not certify arithmetic or bit complexity.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}


Arbitrary measurable sequential adaptive randomized algorithms are allowed. The private seed is independent of the hidden instance. Queries, stopping, and output may use the full history, without additional span, zero-respecting, communication, or memory restrictions.



A single algorithm is chosen from the public input and must satisfy the guarantee for every fixed admissible instance.




\AtlasMath{\Pr\!\left(\max_{v\in\Delta_m}v^\top A\widehat{x}-\min_{u\in X}\widehat{y}^\top Au\le\varepsilon\right)\ge\frac23.}




Probability is over private algorithmic randomness only. The unknown instance is fixed before interaction.



\textbf{Budget convention.} fixed\_worst\_case\_cap



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{2. Notation and parameters}


\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}: Target tolerance for the complete weak-VI gap or global saddle gap, in the units of that gap. \textbf{Domain:} Positive real number.



\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_0}: A sufficiently small accuracy threshold for the randomized matrix lower bound. \textbf{Domain:} Universal positive constant.



\AtlasInlineMath{m}: Number of matrix rows, or equivalently coordinates of the maximizing strategy \textbf{Domain:} Positive integer.



\AtlasInlineMath{n}: The number of matrix columns and minimizing-strategy coordinates. \textbf{Domain:} Positive integer.



\AtlasInlineMath{q}: This integer scale comes from the source randomized hard-instance construction. It is selected through \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon} to specify the dimension window, not an additional oracle budget. \textbf{Domain:} Positive integer.



\AtlasInlineMath{q\asymp\varepsilon^{-2/3}}



\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}: Euclidean norm and inner product; the product-space norm is the square root of the sum of the squared block norms. \textbf{Domain:} The specified finite-dimensional real vector space.



\AtlasInlineMath{\|v\|_2=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}}



\AtlasInlineMath{\widehat x,\widehat y}: The point or variable blocks ultimately returned by the algorithm, corresponding to the hatted variables in the error formula. \textbf{Domain:} Feasible variable pairs in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb R^{d_x}\times\mathbb R^{d_y}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb E,\Pr}: Expectation and probability over the explicitly allowed algorithm and sample randomness, with the hidden instance fixed. \textbf{Domain:} Operations on the corresponding probability space.



\AtlasInlineMath{N_{\rm matvec}}: Number of bundled exact two-sided matrix-vector product calls \textbf{Domain:} Nonnegative integer count; expected work is its expectation.



\AtlasInlineMath{N}: A uniform cap on principal information calls for every admissible instance and execution path. \textbf{Domain:} Nonnegative integer.



\AtlasInlineMath{N^\star}: The infimum principal query budget among algorithms satisfying every stated instancewise output guarantee. \textbf{Domain:} Nonnegative extended real value; by convention, positive infinity if no successful algorithm or no uniform finite budget exists.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal A,I}: An algorithm selected from public inputs and an admissible hidden instance fixed before interaction \textbf{Domain:} The specified algorithm and model classes.



\AtlasInlineMath{\omega}: A complete realization of algorithmic and sample randomness. \textbf{Domain:} Corresponding sample space.



\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde O}: Asymptotic upper and lower bounds, constant-factor matching, and upper bounds hiding the stated logarithmic factors, within the corresponding regions. \textbf{Domain:} Nonnegative complexity function; subscript p permits additional dependence only on fixed p.



\AtlasInlineMath{\log,\ln,\log_+}: Natural logarithm and its nonnegative truncation \textbf{Domain:} Arguments of log and ln are positive; the argument of \AtlasInlineMath{\log_+} may be zero.



\AtlasInlineMath{\log_+(t)=\log(\max\{1,t\})}



\AtlasInlineMath{A}: The hidden payoff matrix has maximizing strategies as rows and minimizing strategies as columns. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{x,y}: Minimization variable and maximization strategy; query vectors need not satisfy strategy constraints \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{x\in\mathbb R^n,\ y\in\mathbb R^m}.



\AtlasInlineMath{X}: The public strategy set of the minimizing variable. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{B_2^n}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Delta_k,\mathbf1}: \AtlasInlineMath{k}-dimensional probability simplex and the all-ones vector of the corresponding dimension \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{k\ge1}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Delta_k=\{u\in\mathbb R^k:u_j\ge0,\ \mathbf1^\top u=1\}}



\AtlasInlineMath{\operatorname{Gap}}: The displayed global saddle gap maximizes and minimizes over the output strategy domains. \textbf{Domain:} Nonnegative real number; not a gradient norm.



\AtlasInlineMath{B_2^k}: Closed k-dimensional Euclidean unit ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{k\ge1}.



\AtlasInlineMath{B_2^k=\{u\in\mathbb R^k:\|u\|_2\le1\}}



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathfrak A_\varepsilon}: Algorithms using the allowed interfaces, algorithm restrictions, and output domain, and satisfying the displayed complete error guarantee for every fixed admissible instance \textbf{Domain:} The algorithm class is defined at fixed public parameters and target tolerance \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\eta}: Public target accuracy used to run the KOS witness; clamping avoids nonpositive precision logarithms. \textbf{Domain:} Real number in (0,1/2].



\AtlasInlineMath{\eta=\min\{\varepsilon,1/2\}}



\AtlasInlineMath{\ell_{\mathrm{KOS}}}: Positive dimension and precision logarithm dominating the polylogarithmic factors in KOS v3. \textbf{Domain:} Positive real number.



\AtlasInlineMath{\ell_{\mathrm{KOS}}=1+\log(2mn/\eta)}

For any normalized A and any y in Delta\_m, choose x=0. The full saddle gap is max\_i (A x)\_i\char45{}min\_\{||u||<=1\} y\textasciicircum{}T A u=||A\textasciicircum{}T y||<=sum\_i y\_i ||A\_i||<=1. Thus zero queries suffice for epsilon>=1, deterministically, in all positive dimensions.
For necessity, fix a unit vector a=e\_1 in R\textasciicircum{}n. Let A\_+ have every row a\textasciicircum{}T and A\_\char45{}=\char45{}A\_+. Every feasible output (x,y) has gaps 1+a\textasciicircum{}T x and 1\char45{}a\textasciicircum{}T x respectively. When epsilon<1, their success events are disjoint. A zero\char45{}query randomized algorithm has the same output law under both fixed matrices. Consequently the two success probabilities sum to at most one, so at least one is at most 1/2<2/3. This proves N*>=1 for any fixed pathwise cap below one. At epsilon=1 the output x=0 succeeds for both and for the whole class; the boundary is closed on the zero side. If min(m,n)=1, the preceding reconstruction proof uses one call and exactly solves every instance. Hence the endpoint complexity is exactly one below 1 and zero at or above 1. No epsilon\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}2/3) lower bound is inferred.

Native pointer: /proofs/3/proof; canonical SHA-256: 830634749b673645bb822c76\allowbreak{}89cfa490ccc3296b39ae23fa\allowbreak{}378ef45c114a7a70


Source premise: Karmarkar\char45{}\char45{}O\char39{}Carroll\char45{}\char45{}Sidford, arXiv:2601.02347v3, Theorem 1.2, states a deterministic algorithm for every normalized game of this type with tilde\char45{}O(eta\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}2/3)) matvecs. Section 1 defines an eta\char45{}solution by the complete saddle gap, and its oracle returns the pair (A\textasciicircum{}T y,Ax). Footnote 3 limits the hidden factors to polylogarithms in m,n,eta\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}1). The source\char39{}s Section 7.2 proof establishes this theorem without a lower bound on dimension depending on eta.

Class/output/metric map: the source class X=B\_2\textasciicircum{}n, Y=Delta\_m and max\_i ||A\_\{i,:\}||\_2<=1 is exactly the present normalized class. Its feasible output pair is a legal target output, and its max\_y y\textasciicircum{}T A xhat \char45{} min\_x yhat\textasciicircum{}T A x metric is the target complete gap. Run the theorem at eta=min\{epsilon,1/2\}. Since eta<=epsilon, its deterministic gap guarantee implies target success probability one, hence at least 2/3, for every fixed admissible matrix. This is a one\char45{}way deterministic\char45{}witness inclusion into the randomized algorithm class; it transfers no deterministic lower bound.

Oracle/cost map: the source pair query is a legal target query because the target allows arbitrary real x,y. One such source pair is answered by exactly one target bundled response (Ax,A\textasciicircum{}T y), with order exchanged internally if needed. A source implementation that requests one directional product can obtain it using one target call with the other vector zero and discard the extra response. If two directions are requested sequentially, charge the actual two calls; do not divide directional counts by two or merge adaptively dependent queries. Thus the source count is an upper bound on target calls, up to at most a fixed convention factor absorbed in C\_KOS. Exact arithmetic, known\char45{}domain optimization, and computation from returned data are free in both query models. The source has a deterministic worst\char45{}case call bound, so its witness satisfies the target pathwise cap; there is no expectation\char45{}to\char45{}cap conversion.

Uniform integer budget: because m,n>=1 and 0<eta<=1/2, the positive quantity ell\_KOS=1+log(2mn/eta) dominates 1, log m, log n and log(1/eta). The source tilde\char45{}O bound can therefore be bounded by C\_KOS eta\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}2/3) ell\_KOS\textasciicircum{}(p\_KOS) for fixed universal C\_KOS>=1 and p\_KOS>=0, increasing the constant for finite endpoint ranges. Round upward to K\_KOS. For m,n>=2 use the source algorithm. When min(m,n)=1, use the separately proved one\char45{}call exact reconstruction instead, which is no greater than K\_KOS. This handles singleton dimensions without relying on an entropy bound with log(1)=0. The choice eta<=1/2 also handles epsilon>=1 and avoids a false vanishing logarithmic factor. All dimensions are finite and positive, and epsilon=0 is outside the native accuracy domain.

Envelope: independently, basis reconstruction costs at most min(m,n) and returns gap zero. Both witnesses are chosen using public dimensions and accuracy, so select the smaller of their public proved integer caps. This proves the displayed min bound directly for q2. The old q1 source\char45{}scoped resource record is not identified with q2, and the old narrow b2 record is not needed for the new envelope. On every nonzero comparison updated here, 0<epsilon<2; consequently epsilon/4<=eta<=epsilon and the same upper is written min\{min(m,n),tilde\char45{}O(epsilon\textasciicircum{}(\char45{}2/3))\}, with only the stated positive dimension/precision logarithms suppressed. Existing exact zero and exact one\char45{}query rows are sharper and remain selected unchanged. This proves only an upper bound; the separate claimed randomized growing lower remains excluded.
